cards.explanation: The answer is the Jews who survived the exile, and Jerusalem. Nehemiah says he questioned the men about "…the remnant of the Jews who had survived the exile, and also about Jerusalem." (Nehemiah 1:2) He wants to know about the people AND the city. I think a man who asks that much cares a whole lot, friends.

The answer is that the wall's broken down and the gates are burned. The men say, "The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire." (Nehemiah 1:3) The wall is down and the gates are burned, friends. That's the news Nehemiah gets.

The answer is True. Nehemiah says, "When I heard these words, I sat down and wept." (Nehemiah 1:4) The news about the wall and the gates hit him hard, and he doesn't hide it. He sits down right there and weeps.
The word is praying. Nehemiah mourned "…for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven." (Nehemiah 1:4) When the news broke his heart, he took it straight to God. Smart man, bakers.

The answer is False. Nehemiah says God "…keeps His covenant of loving devotion with those who love Him and keep His commandments…" (Nehemiah 1:5) He doesn't say every nation on earth, friends. The text names the ones who love God and keep His commandments.

The answer is True. Nehemiah says, "Both I and my father’s house have sinned." (Nehemiah 1:6) He confesses the sins the Israelites have committed, and he counts himself and his father's house in it, bakers.

The answer is False. Nehemiah says, "We have behaved corruptly against You and have not kept the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that You gave Your servant Moses." (Nehemiah 1:7) He says plainly they haven't kept them, friends. That's honest prayer.

The answer is that God will gather them and bring them to His chosen place. God's word says that if they return to Him and keep His commandments, then even if the exiles are banished "…to the farthest horizon, I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I have chosen as a dwelling for My Name." (Nehemiah 1:9) That's a promise of gathering, no matter how far they've been scattered. Nehemiah brings that word up in his prayer, asking God to remember what He told Moses. (Nehemiah 1:8)

The word is mercy. Nehemiah prays, "…grant him mercy in the sight of this man." (Nehemiah 1:11) He's asking God for mercy in the sight of a man, friends. He also asks God to give him success that day.

The answer is cupbearer to the king. Nehemiah adds, "(At that time I was the cupbearer to the king.)" (Nehemiah 1:11) He tucks it in at the very end, bakers, like a little footnote after the prayer. And the story isn't over, because there's more to come with Nehemiah.
